findings.source_passage: you may fancy, for yourself, how it would fare with you, did you sideways survey objects through your ears
findings.source_locator: paragraph on whale's sideway vision, before 'bitterest foe' passage
findings.why_it_matters: This rhetorical invitation — 'you may fancy, for yourself' — is a characteristic Ishmael move drawing the reader into a thought experiment; its absence flattens the narrator's distinctive pedagogical voice before the famous 'bitterest foe' sentence.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'you may fancy, for yourself, how it would fare with you, did you sideways survey objects through your ears' as a lead-in to the bitterest-foe passage.

findings.source_passage: the position of the whale's eyes corresponds to that of a man's ears; and you may fancy, for yourself
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Now, from this peculiar sideway position'
findings.why_it_matters: The analogy 'whale's eyes corresponds to that of a man's ears' is the logical setup that makes the subsequent 'bitterest foe' image legible as argument, not mere rhetoric; dropping it creates a small but real interpretive gap.
findings.suggested_fix: Include the ears/eyes analogy sentence before the thirty-degrees-of-vision detail.

findings.source_passage: which towers between them like a great mountain separating two lakes in valleys
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Moreover, while in most other animals'
findings.why_it_matters: This geological simile is stylistically distinctive and prosodically rich — a classic Melvillean scale-expansion; it is quietly dropped in the draft, which says only 'divided by many cubic feet of head.'
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the mountain/lakes simile when describing the head-mass separating the whale's eyes.

findings.source_passage: alas! it proves to many a poor wight in the fishery, upon whom these spikes fall with impaling force
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'But come out now, and look at this portentous lower jaw'
findings.why_it_matters: The 'poor wight' exclamatory aside is a minor but voice-carrying moment of ironic sympathy; its removal slightly deanimates the jaw description.
findings.suggested_fix: Retain 'alas! it proves to many a poor wight' after the portcullis simile.

findings.source_passage: who must, no doubt, imprecate lock-jaws upon him
findings.source_locator: paragraph on the 'sulky whale' with hanging jaw
findings.why_it_matters: This satirical punchline — imprecating lock-jaws — is a small but characteristic wit-flourish capping the hypochondriac-whale passage; its loss mildly flattens the humour.
findings.suggested_fix: Append 'who must, no doubt, imprecate lock-jaws upon him' to close the sulky-whale passage.

findings.source_passage: furnishing a supply of that hard white whalebone with which the fishermen fashion all sorts of curious articles, including canes, umbrella-stocks, and handles to riding-whips
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'In most cases this lower jaw'
findings.why_it_matters: The catalogue of domestic objects made from whalebone (canes, umbrella-stocks, riding-whips) is a signature inventory — connecting leviathan grandeur to mundane commerce — that Melville deploys throughout; its quiet omission erases that thematic resonance.
findings.suggested_fix: Include the list of whalebone articles (canes, umbrella-stocks, riding-whip handles) in the jaw/dentistry paragraph.

summary: The draft preserves all high-priority signature passages verbatim or near-verbatim, but drops several voice-carrying similes, rhetorical invitations, and ironic asides (mountain/lakes simile, 'you may fancy for yourself,' the lock-jaws punchline, the whalebone-objects catalogue) that together moderately flatten Ishmael's distinctive pedagogical and satirical register without rising to regeneration level.
